slots.body:
Take the health score off the screen at your next renewal review.

Then ask the CSM: “If your sponsor left tomorrow, who would defend this spend?”

Not who attends the QBR. Not who logs in the most. Who would explain to Finance what the company would lose by cutting the contract?

If you can’t name that person, the account can have great adoption and still be a bad bet for the forecast.

I’d ask for three things before calling it commit:
• A recent outcome the customer can describe in their own words.
• A named person who can defend the spend.
• One thing that would make us lower the forecast.

If the answer to the last one is “nothing,” the review isn’t testing the forecast.

What would make you take a green account out of commit?
slots.qa: Author judgement. No personal customer claim or benchmark. No external link.

slots.body:
Your biggest customer doesn't automatically get the next engineer.

Here's a made-up case.

Their export is broken. There's a clumsy workaround. Renewal is close, and they're threatening to leave.

A smaller customer can't complete a core workflow. No workaround. Same support entitlement. One engineer is free.

I'd start with the blocked workflow and put a leader on the phone with the larger customer.

If the renewal threat changes that call, I want us to say whose work we're leaving stopped.

The three-page case is below. Save it for your next escalation review.
slots.asset: One original three-page 4:5 native PDF: Who Gets the Next Engineer.pdf

slots.body:
An AI agent that handles 80% of cases can still make your CX team slower.

Say a manual case takes 10 minutes. The agent clears 80 out of 100. A human spends 3 minutes checking each of those 80. The 20 exceptions take 40 minutes each because someone has to reconstruct what happened.

Before AI: 1,000 human minutes.
After AI: 1,040.

The 80% looks great in a deck. The team just lost 40 minutes.

Before calling a pilot efficient, run the same case twice. First, give the agent enough evidence to act. Then change one fact that should make it stop. See if it spots the difference and hands over enough context that the next person doesn’t have to start again.

Then time the human work all the way to resolution. That’s the number I’d put in front of leadership.
slots.qa: Illustrative arithmetic, not a benchmark or observed customer result:80*3+20*40=1040 versus100*10=1000.

slots.body:
I've led CS teams and built their metrics.

So I'd be wary of promoting someone just because they always know the answer.

A lead who jumps into every difficult customer call can make this week's queue look better. The rest of the team may get fewer chances to learn the job.

For a first-time manager, I'd ask for a different example: a colleague who can now handle something they couldn't handle before.

Who can take that call without them now?

I write about the calls behind leading a CS team. Follow if that's your work too.

slots.body:
The customer shouldn't have to reassure us after we give them bad news.

It's tempting to spend half the call explaining how hard the team has worked.

They may believe us. They still have a deadline to explain.

I'd tell them what they'll be able to do, what they won't, and the next update they can rely on. Then let them be disappointed without asking them to make us feel better.

What would you leave out of that update?
